reviews.author: Brent Marchant
reviews.content: In an age where life’s everyday challenges can test our wits, becoming overwhelmed is a real possibility when they pile up. Just ask Linda (Rose Byrne), a therapist who struggles to sincerely and sensitively assist her troubled patients. But that’s just the start of her problems. She’s also tending to a sick child (Delaney Quinn), the demands of which are considerable, both from the whiny, often-unappreciative youngster and her annoyingly insistent caregivers. To make matters worse, a burst pipe in the ceiling of her apartment has forced mother and child to move into a hotel, a stay that’s become unexpectedly extended due to the lack of repair work by her inattentive landlord. And, through all of these ordeals, Linda is on her own, given that her unfeeling husband (Christian Slater) is frequently away on business. As a consequence, this palette of issues has forced Linda into therapy herself with a peer counselor (Conan O”Brien), whose incessant indifference not only offers little help, but also tends to exacerbate the stress in her life. Over time, the specific pressures associated with each of these incidents begin to snowball, making coping nearly impossible. And, as time passes, Linda feels as though she’s losing herself and descending into her own personal madness. So what is she to do? That’s what this intense offering from actress-writer-director Mary Bronstein seeks to explore. This exceedingly dark comedy-drama examines what a woman on the edge might go through as the breaking point approaches. There’s an undeniably raw, edgy, realistic quality to this release, one that sometimes makes this a decidedly uncomfortable watch. The barrage of challenges to simply get through the day keeps coming at the protagonist (and, hence, viewers) relentlessly, presented here in nonstop fashion at breakneck speed. And it seems that, no matter what good faith efforts Linda makes to resolve her dilemmas, they’re never enough, often exposing her to petty, undue criticism that, in turn, prompt undue, unfair and unfounded accusations of blame and shame. All of these foregoing attributes are routinely intensified by the picture’s regular use of macabre comic relief, serving up laughs about incidents and subjects that many of us might genuinely feel guilty chuckling about. But this film’s real standout asset is the superb performance turned in by Byrne, easily the best work of her career and handily worthy of awards consideration, capably backed by Quinn, O’Brien and other cast members in fine supporting portrayals. To be sure, “If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” won’t suit everyone, and even avid cinephiles may at times find their patience, tolerance and sensibilities sufficiently challenged. Nevertheless, this is one of those “sign of the times” pictures that unflinchingly exposes much of what’s wrong with contemporary society and that we’d all be wise to take seriously if we ever hope to see improvement in a world where a lack of compassion, understanding and support are being allowed to run rampant. It’s no wonder that so many of us might feel like kicking back under conditions like this. Indeed, maybe it’s time we should all seek to grow some legs of our own.

reviews.author: CinemaSerf
reviews.content: Rose Byrne turns in a terrific performance here, but I found the thrust of the plot to be just a bit too much like a contrived horror movie. She is “Linda”, a therapist whose husband is off piloting a boat and whose un-named daughter has some form of undefined illness that is putting huge pressure on her mother. Then, just to add to her woes, a water leak in their apartment turns her ceiling into a Swiss cheese and forces them to take refuge in a rather basic motel. With the sounds of the child’s feeding machine never far from her dreams, “Linda” heads firmly into the realms of a sleep-deprived and booze-induced nervous breakdown that her own psychiatrist (Conan O’Brien) is unable to help with. She is steadily losing the plot, and so are we. Just what is going on with the woman, and with her faceless offspring? At times this is quite an intensely written and potent observation of mental stress and Byrne really does manage to convey her character’s increasing hysteria quite compellingly, but there are too many pieces of the puzzle missing for us to make any meaningful assessment or to do really much more than recoil from her predicament. A little sense of the proceedings is made right at the very end, but by then I had become too lost, and actually disinterested, in it’s maelstrom of despair. The film does convey quite a powerful message about the importance of listening, and of the frustrations and dangers of not listening, but too many of the ancillary characters are either absent, undercooked or just simplistically portrayed - personally or via the telephone, as little more than excuses for her character to present us with someone ostensibly abandoned by those who might and should want to care for her. In the end it came down to a lack of plausibility for me as it built to a conclusion that became a little more expected as we got to know more about “Linda”. It is worth a look, but really only for a Byrne at the top of her game.

reviews.author: badelf
reviews.content:
With truly sincere apologies to Almodóvar, the alternate title to this film could be "Woman in the Throes of a Nervous Breakdown." Mary Bronstein's debut feature captures the absolute insanity of raising a child in this time and place with such visceral precision that watching it feels less like cinema and more like surviving someone else's panic attack in real time.

Rose Byrne plays Linda, a therapist whose life is disintegrating on every front: a child with a mysterious illness requiring a feeding tube, an absent husband, a missing person case, and her own increasingly hostile therapy sessions with a colleague played by Conan O'Brien. Byrne is so devastatingly good in this role that it becomes genuinely difficult to tell if she's acting or actually stuck in the situation. Every frayed nerve, every moment of barely controlled hysteria, every attempt to hold it together while everything falls apart feels utterly, uncomfortably real. This is fearless work, the kind of performance that makes you wonder what it costs to go to those places.

The soundtrack and sound design, crafted by Filipe Messeder with re-mixing by Ruy Garcia, function as the film's true co-star. This is genuinely unique and original work; Bronstein and her sound team use audio not just to underscore Linda's mental state but to replicate it. The soundscape becomes oppressive, intrusive, relentless in ways that mirror the demands of parenthood, the medical system, professional obligations, the voice in your head telling you you're failing at everything simultaneously. It's brilliant, suffocating filmmaking.

There's a pointed meta-story here about therapists being unable to manage their own children and lives, about the particular irony of spending your professional life helping others navigate crisis while drowning in your own. Linda dispenses wisdom she can't apply, maintains boundaries she can't sustain, performs competence while unraveling. It's a sharp observation about the helping professions, about the gap between what we know intellectually and what we can actually do when our own world is on fire.

Bronstein's vision here establishes her as a director to watch. She refuses to soften the edges, refuses to provide easy catharsis or reassuring resolution. This is horror filmmaking in the truest sense; not jump scares or supernatural threats, but the genuine terror of feeling your grip on sanity slipping while still being expected to function, to parent, to show up. It's the kind of film that makes some viewers want children even less and makes parents feel seen in ways that are both validating and destabilizing.

If I Had Legs is genuinely hard to watch, a masterwork of psychological horror that understands motherhood as the impossible task it often is, performed with courage by Byrne and directed with uncompromising vision by Bronstein. 10/10

aiEnrichment.summary_one_sentence: Overwhelmed by her young daughter's severe feeding disorder and an absent husband, psychotherapist Linda spirals into psychological burnout as her personal and professional lives violently collide.
aiEnrichment.summary_short: Linda is a worn-down psychotherapist whose life rapidly unravels under overwhelming personal and logistical pressures. While acting as the sole caregiver for her young daughter who suffers from a complex pediatric feeding disorder, her apartment ceiling unexpectedly collapses, forcing them into a temporary motel stay. Compounded by demanding therapy clients and a distant husband who criticizes her from afar, Linda pushes herself beyond her emotional limits. Her chaotic journey explores the harrowing realities of isolation, maternal responsibility, and mental exhaustion.
aiEnrichment.summary_long: Linda, a practicing psychotherapist, struggles to manage an increasingly chaotic life while acting as the sole daily caretaker for her young daughter. Her child suffers from a severe pediatric feeding disorder that requires daily hospital visits and nightly tube feedings, leaving Linda perpetually exhausted. Her husband is away working as a ship captain, offering little real assistance and instead criticizing her over distant phone calls. The situation turns dire when a major leak causes her apartment ceiling to cave in, driving Linda and her daughter to live out of a motel. At work, Linda's emotional reserve breaks down, impacting her ability to effectively treat her patients. During one volatile session, an anxious patient abruptly runs off and abandons her baby in Linda's care, pushing Linda even closer to the edge. Escaping into late-night walks, Linda forms brief, unpredictable encounters with a fellow motel guest while seeking relief. As her relationships with her family, patients, and her own therapist rapidly deteriorate, Linda is forced to confront her deepest fears and complete psychological exhaustion. Ultimately, the film charts a gripping and unfiltered collapse of a woman trying to hold everything together against impossible odds.
aiEnrichment.synopsis: Directed by Mary Bronstein, *If I Had Legs I'd Kick You* is a tense and raw psychological drama following Linda (Rose Byrne), a mother and psychotherapist pushed to her absolute limit. Facing the intense demands of managing her child's complex feeding illness without support from her long-distance husband, Linda's life takes a turn for the worse when home structural issues displace them to a local motel. As the boundaries between her duty to her patients and her own crumbling mental stability begin to blur, Linda navigates an unflinching, darkly comic, and emotional exploration of maternal overload, isolation, and burnout.
